newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines seen surviving attacks on currency.
newsitem.headline: Philippines seen surviving attacks on currency.

text.p: The volatile Philippine peso stabilised on Thursday, lifting market confidence in the central bank's ability to wrestle currency speculators.
Manila bankers said the central bank appeared well equipped to ward off future attacks against the currency, which has suffered heavy selling pressure in tandem with the recently devalued Thai baht.
"It looks like the (peso) has stabilised... It did not take much to fend off speculators," Bankers Association of the Philippines president Deogracias Vistan told reporters.
Vistan is also the president of Solid Banking Corp.
The peso tumbled on Wednesday on brisk selling by speculators and foreign fund managers shortly after Thai authorities announced a managed float of the baht.

That selling drove the currency to 26.380 to the dollar from 26.374 on Tuesday, forcing the Central Bank to support the peso with a hike in its overnight borrowing rate to 24 percent from 15 percent and heavy currency intervention.
By Thursday morning, the peso had steadied to between 26.403 and 26.405.

"I don't think the speculation will continue because the Central Bank has effectively intervened by raising the overnight interest rate," Philippine National Bank president Peter Favila said in a separate interview.
Philippine Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson said the benchmark interest rate would be lowered once the jitters from the Thai financial crisis died down.
"As things settle down, as speculations stop, we will start pulling down the rate," he said.
While the peso, along with other regional currencies, still remained vulnerable to further speculative selling, industry leaders said the Central Bank should be able to protect the local currency.
"If we were to go by the record of the Central Bank, they've been successful in this type of intervention," Favila said.
But some see the peso as the next natural target for speculators following the devaluation of the Thai baht.
"Clearly the peso will be the main target now," Manu Bhaskaran, head of research at SocGen-Crosby Securities, told a briefing in Singapore on Thursday.
"It is the one (other) currency in Southeast Asia which we would see as overvalued. The natural pressures could see some correction...perhaps five or six percent over six months."
By the end of 1997, he expected the peso to be around 28.50.
Bhaskaran said the peso was vulnerable because the country's foreign exchange reserves were not as strong as some of its neighbours and its balance of payments had weakened in recent months.
But Vistan said strong macroeconomic fundamentals would help shore up the peso in the long run.

The Central Bank had adopted the same two-pronged strategy -- raising rates and aggressively selling dollars -- in defending the peso in January 1995 when the Mexican financial debacle spilled over to Asia's emerging markets.
Rafael Buenaventura, president of Philippine Commercial International Bank, said the country's floating exchange rate regime had made the central bank's task easier.
"We are not married to a pegged exchange rate... The job of the Central Bank is just to remove huge fluctuations in the exchange rate," Buenaventura said.
"If the exchange rate is under pressure because of the normal demand, it will let the market determine the rate."
Singson said he remained confident the Central Bank could win future battles against speculators, despite the country's relatively small foreign exchange reserves.

"Our reserves are not our principal weapon to defend the currency against speculative attack. It is the interest rate... Remember Mexico? We reacted primarily by increasing the overnight interest rate. That worked, didn't it?" Singson said.
The Philippine peso came under similar attack in January 1995 forcing the Central Bank to raise its overnight rate to as high as 30 percent, effectively stamping out further speculation.
